title: PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
text:
0.1 Scope
PGM — Practical Growth Models is a jamovi module for fitting, evaluating, and interpreting nonlinear growth curves.
The module provides tools for:
PGM is intended for researchers analyzing longitudinal or cross-sectional growth data in animal science, plant science, microbiology, ecology, developmental biology, and related fields.
The documentation is divided into four main parts:

title: PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
text:
0.2 Important considerations
PGM assists with model estimation and interpretation but does not replace statistical judgment. Model selection should not be based on a single goodness-of-fit statistic. The adequacy of the mean function, residual variance, dependence structure, parameter plausibility, and residual diagnostics should be considered jointly.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Why use parametric growth models?
Growth is a dynamic process in which the size, mass, concentration, or other measurable characteristic of a biological system changes over time.
Sigmoidal growth models summarize an entire trajectory using a small number of parameters related to characteristics such as:
PGM provides a graphical interface for fitting these models in jamovi, while retaining statistical procedures commonly implemented in R.
Parametric growth models can provide interpretable summaries of nonlinear trajectories. Depending on the selected model, their parameters may describe:
These interpretations depend on the equation and parametrization used. Parameters with similar names are not necessarily equivalent across different growth models.

3  Installation
text:
3.1 Installing jamovi
PGM is an add-on module for jamovi. Before installing the module, download and install the current version of jamovi from its official website.
After installation, open jamovi and verify that the main analysis interface is working correctly.

title: 3  Installation
section: 3.2 Installing PGM from the jamovi library
text:
3.2 Installing PGM from the jamovi library
PGM is available in the official jamovi library:

Open jamovi.
Select the Modules icon, in the upper-right of Analysis menu.
Open the jamovi module library.
Search for PGM.
Select Install.

After installation, PGM will appear in the main analysis ribbon.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.3 Installing a development version
Development versions may be distributed as .jmo files on PGM GitHub repository.

To install a local module:
Open jamovi.
Select the Modules icon.
Select Sideload.
Locate the .jmo file.
Confirm the installation.

Development versions may contain recently added features that have not yet been included in a stable release.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.4 Updating PGM
When PGM is installed through the jamovi library, available updates can be installed through the module manager.
For reproducible academic work, record the PGM and jamovi versions.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.5 Verifying the installation
After installation, open a dataset containing numeric time and response variables. The module includes example datasets for testing and learning purposes. They are available from the jamovi menu in the upper-left corner: Open → Data Library → PGM.
Next, select Growth from the analysis ribbon and open Curve Modeling. Assign at least one response variable and one time variable.
If the analysis interface opens and produces an initial result, the module has been installed successfully.

4  Data preparation
text:
4.1 Example datasets
The module includes example datasets derived from published studies for testing and learning purposes. References for the original data sources are provided with each dataset.
They are available from the jamovi menu in the upper-left corner: Open → Data Library → PGM.

4.2 Basic structure
Data should be provided in long format, with one row per observation.
At minimum, the dataset must contain:

one numeric response variable;
one numeric time or age variable.

For longitudinal analyses, the dataset must also contain:

one identification variable indicating the experimental unit or subject.

title: 4  Data preparation
text:
4.5 Variable requirements

4.5.1 Response
The response must be numeric and should represent a cumulative or monotonic biological growth process when a sigmoidal growth model is used.


4.5.2 Time
Time must be numeric. Examples include:

age in days;
age in weeks;
hours after inoculation;
days after planting.

The unit of time determines the unit of rate parameters and derivative quantities.


4.5.3 Subject identifier
The subject identifier may be numeric or categorical. It is used to associate repeated observations with the same experimental unit.
Selecting an identifier changes the statistical model from an ordinary or generalized nonlinear model to a nonlinear mixed-effects model.

title: 4  Data preparation
text:
4.6 Missing observations
Rows containing missing values in variables required by a given analysis are excluded from that analysis.
Different response variables may therefore be fitted using different numbers of observations.

title: 4  Data preparation
text:
4.7 Measurement schedule
For models using discrete AR(1) residual correlation, equally spaced observations are generally expected.
For irregularly spaced measurements, continuous-time CAR(1) correlation is usually more appropriate.

title: 4  Data preparation
5  Running an analysis
text:
5.1 Opening the analysis
To begin:
Each modeling setup defines the response variable, growth model, residual variance structure, and residual correlation structure to be used in that analysis.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
Open the dataset in jamovi.
Select PGM from the analysis ribbon.
Open the growth-curve analysis.
Assign the time variable.
Assign one or more response variables.
Add a modeling setup for each response-model combination.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.2 Selecting the response
The response should be numeric and should represent a process compatible with the selected growth equation.
Examples include: body weight; organism size; microbial concentration; plant height; cumulative production; other continuous responses measured over time.
A sigmoidal growth model should not be selected solely because the observations increase over time. The observed trajectory should also exhibit a biologically and statistically plausible sigmoidal form.

title: 5  Running an analysis
5  Running an analysis
text:
5.4 Subject identifier
For repeated measurements, assign a subject or experimental-unit identifier.
When no identifier is supplied, observations are treated as independent.
When an identifier is supplied, PGM fits a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which repeated observations are grouped within subjects.
The identifier should represent the unit that generates the repeated trajectory, such as: animal; plant; patient; experimental vessel; microbial batch; plot.
Treatment group, sex, breed, or experimental condition should not be used as the subject identifier unless each category genuinely represents one repeated observational unit.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.5 Selecting a model
Choose the growth equation according to: the expected trajectory shape; parameter interpretability; biological context; data coverage; convergence; residual diagnostics; comparative model performance.
Different equations may fit similarly while producing parameters with different meanings.
The current version fits only the 4-parameter Richards, that should cover the shapes of both Gompertz and Logistic models.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.6 Selecting a residual variance structure
Use a variance function when residual spread changes systematically with the fitted response.
Available structures may include:

constant variance;
power variance;
exponential variance;
constant-plus-power variance.

The selection should be supported by residual diagnostics and comparative model evaluation.
Selecting residual correlation
Residual correlation structures are available for longitudinal analyses.
Use:
AR(1) when measurements are approximately equally spaced and correlation is interpreted by measurement lag; CAR(1) when measurement intervals are irregular and correlation depends on the actual temporal distance.
Random effects and residual autocorrelation represent different dependence mechanisms and may be included simultaneously.

title: 5  Running an analysis
5  Running an analysis
6  Overview
text:
6.1 Estimation pathways
PGM selects the estimation framework according to the structure of the data and the analysis options.
All estimation pathways begin with an initial nonlinear fit using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Elzhov et al. 2023).
When a residual variance function is selected without a subject identifier, the initial estimates are used to initialize a generalized nonlinear least-squares model (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
When a subject identifier is selected, the initial estimates are used to initialize a nonlinear mixed-effects model (Pinheiro et al. 2026).

6.3 Maximum likelihood
Nonlinear mixed-effects models in PGM are estimated using maximum likelihood.
This facilitates comparisons between nested models with different fixed effects, provided that the models use the same response, observations, and likelihood framework.

Pinheiro, José, Douglas Bates, and R Core Team. 2026. nlme: Linear and Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.nlme.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.1 General formulation
A parametric growth model represents the expected response at time \(t\) as
\[y_i = W(t_i;\boldsymbol\theta) + \varepsilon_i,\]
where:
\(W(t_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\) is the selected growth function; \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is the vector of model parameters; \(\varepsilon_i\) is the residual error.
The interpretation of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) depends on the exact equation and parametrization.
Models with similar names may be expressed using different parameter definitions in different authors and software implementations.

title: 7  Growth Models
7  Growth Models
text:
7.3 Richards model
PGM implements the Richards parametrization described by Tjørve and Tjørve (2010).
The growth function is
\[A
\left[
1+
(d-1)
\exp\left(
-\frac{K(t-T_i)}
{d^{d/(1-d)}}
\right)
\right]^{1/(1-d)}.\]
The parameters are:

\(A\): asymptotic response;
\(K\): growth-rate parameter under this parametrization;
\(T_i\): time at the inflection point;
\(d\): shape parameter controlling curve asymmetry.

The meaning of \(K\) is specific to this parametrization and should not be assumed to equal the rate parameter of another Richards equation.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.4 Parameter constraints
PGM fits the Richards model using transformed parameters:
\[A=\exp(\alpha),\]
\[K=\exp(\kappa),\]
and
\[d=1.05+\exp(\delta).\]
Consequently: \[
(A>0); (K>0); (d>1.05).
\] The \(d>1.05\) restriction is part of the current computational implementation and restricts the range of Richards shapes that can be fitted.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.5 Starting values
Starting values are generated automatically from the observed trajectory.
The initial asymptote is based on a value above the observed maximum response. The initial inflection time is informed by the largest numerical growth rate, and the initial rate parameter is derived from that rate relative to the initial asymptote.




Tjørve, Even, and Kathleen M. C. Tjørve. 2010. “A Unified Approach to the Richards-Model Family for Use in Growth Analyses: Why We Need Only Two Model Forms.” Journal of Theoretical Biology 267 (3): 417–25. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2010.09.008.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.1 Initial nonlinear fit
PGM first fits the selected growth equation using nonlinear least squares and the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Elzhov et al. 2023).
The initial fit serves two purposes:
Starting values are generated automatically from the observed data and the selected growth model.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
it provides estimates for an ordinary nonlinear analysis;
it supplies starting values for generalized nonlinear least-squares or nonlinear mixed-effects estimation.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.2 Parameter transformations
Some models are fitted using transformed parameters to impose parameter constraints and improve numerical stability.
For example, a positive parameter \(A\) may be represented internally as
\[A = \exp(\alpha).\]
The reported estimate is returned to the natural parameter scale.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.3 Standard errors
The covariance matrix is initially obtained on the transformed estimation scale.
For parameters reported after nonlinear back-transformation, uncertainty is propagated to the natural scale using a first-order delta method.
If \(\boldsymbol\theta\) denotes the transformed parameters and \(g(\boldsymbol\theta)\) their natural-scale representation, then
\[\operatorname{Var}\!\left[g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\right]
\approx
J
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})
J^\mathsf{T},\]
where \(J\) is the Jacobian matrix of the back-transformation.

title: 8  Estimation
9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.1 When mixed effects are used
A nonlinear mixed-effects model is fitted when a subject identification variable is supplied (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
The model separates:

title: 9  Mixed Effects
9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.2 Current random-effects structure
In the current implementation, the asymptotic parameter \(A\) contains an individual random effect.
On the transformed scale, the subject-specific asymptote may be written as
\[\log(A_i) = \log(A) + b_{Ai},\]
where
\[b_{Ai} \sim N(0,\sigma_A^2).\]
All remaining growth parameters are treated as fixed population parameters.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.3 Interpretation
The fixed asymptotic parameter represents the population-level central trajectory on the model scale.
The random effect represents persistent between-individual variation in the asymptotic level.
Residual error represents observation-level variation remaining after accounting for the fixed effects, random effects, variance function, and residual correlation structure.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.4 Conditional fitted values
Residual diagnostics for nonlinear mixed-effects models use conditional fitted values. These include the estimated individual random effects.
Consequently, the diagnostic residuals describe fit to individual trajectories rather than only to the population-average trajectory.




Pinheiro, José, Douglas Bates, and R Core Team. 2026. nlme: Linear and Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.nlme.

title: 10  Variance Functions
text:
10.1 Power variance function
Ordinary nonlinear least squares assumes constant residual variance:
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2.\]
This assumption is often unrealistic for biological growth data because larger responses may exhibit greater absolute variability.
PGM provides alternative residual variance functions based on the fitted response \(\hat y_i\).
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2 |\hat y_i|^{2\theta}.\]
Interpretation:

title: 10  Variance Functions
10  Variance Functions
text:
10.2 Exponential variance function
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2 \exp(2\theta\hat y_i).\]
This model represents an exponential relationship between residual standard deviation and fitted response.

title: 10  Variance Functions
text:
10.3 Constant-plus-power variance function
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2
\left(
\theta_1 + |\hat y_i|^{\theta_2}
\right)^2.\]
This structure permits a nonzero baseline component together with a power-related increase or decrease in residual variation.

title: 10  Variance Functions
11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.1 AR(1)
Repeated observations from the same subject may remain correlated even after individual random effects are included.
PGM provides first-order discrete and continuous-time correlation structures.
For observations separated by \(h\) measurement steps,
\[\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{i,t},\varepsilon_{i,t+h})
=
\phi^{|h|},\]
where \(-1 < \phi < 1\).
AR(1) is most naturally interpreted when observations are ordered and approximately equally spaced.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.2 CAR(1)
For observations made at times \(t\_{ij}\) and \(t\_{ik}\),
\[\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{ik})
=
\phi^{|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|}.\]
CAR(1) uses the actual temporal distance between observations and is therefore suitable for irregularly spaced measurements.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.3 Random effects are not autocorrelation
Random effects and residual correlation represent different sources of dependence.
A random effect represents persistent individual differences in the growth trajectory.
Residual autocorrelation represents association between observation-level departures occurring close together in time.
A model may require one, both, or neither structure.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.1 Derivative notation
Let \(W(t)\) denote the fitted growth function.
PGM may calculate:
\[W'(t),\]
the instantaneous growth rate, and
\[W''(t),\]
the growth acceleration.
Higher-order derivatives are used for selected geometric descriptors.
These quantities are properties of the fitted curve and inherit any misspecification or uncertainty in the underlying growth model.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.2 Inflection point
The inflection point is identified from a sign change in the second derivative:
\[W''(t)=0.\]
At the inflection point of a standard sigmoidal trajectory, the growth rate is at its maximum.
When no sign change is found within the evaluated interval, PGM reports that no inflection point was detected.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.3 Acceleration extrema
Following Gregorczyk (1991), PGM defines:

\(P1\): time of maximum positive growth acceleration before the inflection point;
\(P2\): time of minimum, or most negative, growth acceleration after the inflection point.

Thus, \[\arg\max_{t<T_i} W''(t),\] and \[\arg\min_{t>T_i} W''(t).\]
These points describe the transition from increasing acceleration toward maximum growth rate and the subsequent period of strongest deceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.4 Ontogenetic growth force
The ontogenetic growth force is defined as in Garcia-Neto et al. (2020):
\[W'(t)W''(t).\]
PGM may report:

\(F1\): maximum OGF before the inflection point;
\(F2\): the inflection-point location represented in the OGF sequence;

Because \(W'(t)\) is nonnegative for an increasing growth trajectory, the sign of OGF generally follows the sign of \(W''(t)\).
OGF-based points consider the magnitude of growth rate in the transition points from acceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.5 Effective growth onset
Available onset descriptors may include:

\(Tan.\): tangent-based onset;
\(Thr.\): threshold-based onset;
\(PAA\): Acceleration-derived onset;
\(F0\): OGF-derived onset.


12.5.1 Tangent method
The tangent method uses the tangent line at the point of maximum growth rate and calculates its intersection with the baseline response represented by the fitted value at the beginning of the evaluated interval.
Its result depends on the observed or selected lower time boundary.


12.5.2 Threshold method
The threshold method identifies the first time at which the fitted trajectory reaches a selected proportion of its fitted late-stage value.
The result depends directly on the chosen threshold.


12.5.3 Absolute Acceleration Point
PAA is identified before \(P1\) from a zero crossing of the fourth derivative of the growth function (Korkmaz et al. 2018).
It represents a transition in the evolution of growth acceleration.


12.5.4 OGF-derived onset
The OGF-derived onset is calculated using the third derivative of the OGF before \(P1\).
It represents a transition in the evolution of the weighted growth acceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.6 Late-growth descriptors
Available late-stage descriptors may include:

\(F3\): an OGF-derived late point;
\(PDA\): Point of Asymptotic Deceleration (Mischan et al. 2011).

These are identified after \(P2\) using derivative-based rules.
They indicate geometric transitions toward the late portion of the fitted trajectory. From that point, growth acceleration decreases very slowly, as it asymptotically approach zero (Mischan et al. 2011).

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.7 Integral descriptors
PGM may calculate the area under the curve (AUC) for the fitted growth function and its first derivative.
It may be useful to summarize growth “intensity” in a single metric across different trajectories (treatments, lineages, or other factors). Comparisons require the same time unit, response unit, interval, and fitted-variable definition.
The area under the fitted growth curve:
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U} W(t),dt.\]
It may also calculate the integrated squared growth rate:
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U}
\left[W'(t)\right]^2dt,\]
and the response-weighted integrated squared growth rate (Garcia-Neto et al. 2020):
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U}
W(t)\left[W'(t)\right]^2dt.\]
If a custom integration interval is not provided, the AUC will be calculated for the complete time vector provided.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.8 Numerical evaluation
Critical points are located on a dense time grid spanning the fitted interval.
Consequently, their reported precision is affected by the numerical grid resolution and should not be interpreted as exact analytic precision.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.9 Uncertainty
The current critical-point and integral tables provide point estimates.
Confidence intervals for derived times and integral descriptors are not automatically implied by confidence intervals for the model parameters.
Bootstrap, simulation, or delta-method procedures would be required to quantify their uncertainty separately.




Garcia-Neto, M., E. Kebreab, and M. J. A. Faria-Junior. 2020. PPFM: Practical Program for Forces Modeling. Software spreadsheet. https://sites.google.com/view/ppfm-spreadsheet/.


Gregorczyk, Andrzej. 1991. “The Logistic Function—Its Application to the Description and Prognosis of Plant Growth.” Acta Societatis Botanicorum Poloniae 60 (1–2): 67–76. https://doi.org/10.5586/asbp.1991.004.


Korkmaz, Mehmet, Volkan Oda, and Elif Ozkurt Basustaoglu. 2018. “A Study over Determination of Asymptotic Deceleration and Absolute Acceleration Points in Logistic Growth Model.” Turkish Journal of Mathematics and Computer Science 10: 33–37. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tjmcs/article/448246.


Mischan, M. M., S. Z. Pinho, and L. R. Carvalho. 2011. “Determination of a Point Sufficiently Close to the Asymptote in Nonlinear Growth Functions.” Scientia Agricola 68 (1): 109–14. https://doi.org/10.1590/S0103-90162011000100016.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.1 Estimation information
The estimation-information table describes the computational and statistical framework used for each modeling setup.
Depending on the selected options, it may report:
This table should be consulted before reporting the model because the same mean equation may be fitted under different residual and dependence assumptions.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.4 Goodness-of-fit measures

13.4.1 Akaike information criterion
The Akaike information criterion is \[-2\ell + 2k,\]
where \(\ell\) is the maximized log-likelihood and \(k\) is the number of estimated parameters counted by the fitted likelihood.
Lower AIC values indicate better expected predictive information performance among comparable models.
The absolute AIC value is not interpreted independently.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.1 Bayesian information criterion
The Bayesian information criterion is \[-2\ell+k\log(n).\]
BIC generally penalizes model complexity more strongly than AIC as the sample size increases.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.2 Descriptive coefficient of determination
PGM calculates \[1-
\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}
{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}.\]
This is a descriptive residual-based statistic on the response scale.
For nonlinear mixed-effects models, it should not be described as the marginal or conditional \(R^2\) commonly defined specifically for mixed models.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.3 Adjusted descriptive coefficient of determination
PGM calculates an adjusted form based on residual degrees of freedom: \[1-
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)}
{\mathrm{SST}/(n-1)}.\]
Its interpretation remains descriptive.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.4 Error metrics

14.4.1 Root mean squared error
\[\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_i
(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
}.\]
RMSE uses the response unit and is relatively sensitive to large residuals.


14.4.2 Relative RMSE
\[\frac{\mathrm{RMSE}}{\bar y}.\]
RRMSE is dimensionless but may behave poorly when the response mean is close to zero.


14.4.3 Mean absolute error
\[\frac{1}{n}
\sum_i
|y_i-\hat y_i|.\]


14.4.4 Median absolute error
\[\operatorname{median}
\left(
|y_i-\hat y_i|
\right).\]
MedAE is less sensitive to isolated large residuals than RMSE or MAE.


14.4.5 Symmetric mean absolute percentage error
PGM calculates \[\frac{100}{n}
\sum_i
\frac{2|y_i-\hat y_i|}
{|y_i|+|\hat y_i|}.\]
A small numerical safeguard is used when both the observed and fitted values are close to zero.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.1 Residuals versus fitted values
PGM provides a four-panel residual diagnostic display.
This plot is used to investigate:
A satisfactory pattern should be centered near zero without pronounced systematic structure.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
14  Residual diagnostics
14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.3 Normal Q–Q plot
The Q–Q plot compares the empirical residual distribution with the normal distribution.
Large systematic departures from the diagonal may indicate skewness, heavy tails, outliers, or model misspecification.
Minor departures should not be interpreted mechanically, particularly with large datasets.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.4 Residual autocorrelation
The autocorrelation plot assesses whether residuals remain associated across neighboring measurement occasions.
For longitudinal models, residual autocorrelation is evaluated within subjects.
Persistent residual autocorrelation may indicate that the selected random effects or residual correlation structure is insufficient.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.5 Residual scale
For generalized nonlinear and nonlinear mixed-effects models, PGM uses normalized residuals that account for the fitted variance and correlation structure.
For ordinary nonlinear least squares, raw residuals are standardized by the estimated residual standard deviation.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.3 Ordinary nonlinear model
A possible methods statement is:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. The [Richards] growth equation was estimated by nonlinear least squares, with initial optimization performed using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm. Model adequacy was evaluated using parameter estimates, information criteria, prediction-error measures, and residual diagnostics.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.4 Generalized nonlinear least squares
When a variance function is included:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. The [Richards] growth equation was estimated by nonlinear least squares, with initial optimization performed using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm. The resulting estimates were used to initialize a generalized nonlinear least-squares model with a [power/exponential/constant-plus-power] residual variance function based on the fitted response.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.5 Nonlinear mixed-effects model
For longitudinal data:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. Repeated growth measurements were analyzed using a nonlinear mixed-effects model. Population growth parameters were represented by fixed effects, and between-subject variation in the asymptotic parameter was represented by a random effect. Parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood after initialization using a Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear fit.


17.5.1 Residual autocorrelation
When applicable:

Within-subject residual dependence was modeled using a first-order [AR(1)/CAR(1)] correlation structure.

For CAR(1), the report may clarify:

Correlation was modeled as a function of the actual temporal distance between observations.



17.5.2 Heteroscedasticity
When applicable:

Residual variance was modeled as a [power/exponential/constant-plus-power] function of the absolute fitted response.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.6 Model comparison
A possible statement is:

Candidate specifications were compared using [AIC/AICc] and BIC, together with residual diagnostics and biological plausibility of the estimated parameters. Information criteria were compared only across models fitted to the same response observations.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.7 Derived growth descriptors
When reporting derivative-based descriptors:

Derived growth values and times were calculated from the fitted growth function and its derivatives, presented as point estimates. These quantities were treated as model-based geometric descriptors.
